title: THEY WALKED OUT OF THEIR GRAVES
paragraphs:
THEY WALKED OUT OF THEIR GRAVES
The Forgotten Resurrection That Shook Jerusalem
The sky turned black in the middle of the day.
The temple veil ripped from top to bottom.
And somewhere beneath the streets of Jerusalem...
Most Christians know about the crucifixion.
Most know about the resurrection of Jesus.

But hidden inside Matthew's Gospel is one of the most astonishing events in all of Scripture—an event so supernatural that if it appeared anywhere outside the Bible, many would dismiss it as impossible.
Yet Matthew records it as history.

And if we truly understand why dead people walked through Jerusalem after Jesus died, we will discover something breathtaking about who Jesus really is, what happened on the cross, and what it means for every grave that has ever been dug.
Two verses that have sparked questions for nearly two thousand years.
Why does only Matthew mention it?
What was God trying to show the world?
To understand this mystery, we must stand beneath the shadow of the cross.
The moment Jesus died was not merely the death of a righteous man.
It was not merely the execution of a prophet.
It was not simply the suffering of a martyr.
Something that shook both heaven and earth.
"Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up His spirit."
Jesus was not overpowered by death.
"No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself."
The cross was not a defeat.
The King was entering enemy territory.
The One who created life was walking directly into death itself.
And death had no idea what was about to happen.
Throughout Scripture, death is portrayed as humanity's great enemy.
The Hebrew word most often associated with the realm of the dead is:
The domain where mankind descends after death.
For generations, every king, prophet, warrior, and servant eventually entered Sheol.
Notice he does not call death a friend.
He does not call death natural.
And at Calvary, the final battle began.
When Matthew describes tombs opening, he is announcing something larger than a miracle.
He is declaring that death's prison doors have been breached.
Imagine a dictator whose fortress has stood unconquered for thousands of years.
No army has ever penetrated its walls.
Then suddenly the gates explode outward.
The fortress has not merely been challenged.
That is the image Matthew wants us to see.
The opening tombs were not random.
Many scholars notice an important detail in Matthew's wording.
The saints did not emerge immediately after Jesus died.
Because Scripture is clear that Jesus is first.
The first portion of a harvest offered to God.
Under Israel's harvest system, the firstfruits guaranteed the larger harvest that would follow.
The saints who appeared in Jerusalem were not competing with Christ.
The truth is Scripture does not tell us.
And biblical honesty requires us to stop where Scripture stops.
Some have speculated that they were prophets.
Others suggest righteous Israelites known throughout Jerusalem.
Still others believe they may have included figures who had recently died and could be recognized by family and friends.
What mattered was not their identity.
What mattered was the One who raised them.
The miracle points away from the saints and toward Jesus.
This is crucial because many modern readers become fascinated by the resurrected people while missing Matthew's central message.
The miracle was never about them.
The reign of death was breaking apart.
There is another detail many readers miss.
Matthew describes real appearances observed by real people.
Jerusalem was filled with Passover pilgrims.
Matthew presents this event as public evidence that something unprecedented had occurred.
Then comes the question everyone asks.
The Bible does not explicitly say.
Because Scripture reserves the ultimate immortal resurrection for the future resurrection of believers.
These saints appear similar to Lazarus.
Raised temporarily as signs of divine power.
Yet even if they later died again, their appearance served a purpose far greater than extending earthly life.
They became living announcements of a coming reality.
Previews of what Christ would accomplish for all who belong to Him.
Because Matthew's strange little account is not ultimately about dead people walking through Jerusalem.
The resurrection of these saints was a preview trailer for the coming kingdom.
A glimpse into a future where cemeteries do not get the final word.
A future where gravestones become temporary markers.
A future where death itself dies.
When Jesus stood before the tomb of Lazarus, He declared:
"I am the resurrection and the life."
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
"I AM the resurrection and the life."
Notice He does not merely give resurrection.
Where Jesus is present, death's authority collapses.
This explains why graves opened when He died.
The Author of Life had entered death's territory.
The darkness could not hold Him.
The grave could not hold Him.
And because it could not hold Him...
it will not hold His people forever either.
Maybe that is why Matthew includes these two mysterious verses.
Hope for every believer standing beside a fresh grave wondering if this is really the end.
The dead walking through Jerusalem were God's announcement that Easter was bigger than one empty tomb.
It was the opening movement of a coming resurrection for all who belong to Christ.
The saints who stepped from their graves were whispers of a future shout.
A preview of the day when Jesus returns.
A preview of the day when every believer hears His voice.
A preview of the day when death finally loses.
The graves around Jerusalem opened because the grave of Jesus would not stay closed.
And because His grave did not stay closed...
Maybe you needed that reminder today.
Maybe you've buried someone you loved.
Maybe you're carrying grief nobody sees.
Maybe you've wondered whether death really has the final word.
Matthew answers with thunder from an earthquake, an empty tomb, and saints walking through Jerusalem.
And one day every cemetery on earth will become a testimony that Christ kept His promise.
The graves opened in Jerusalem because heaven was announcing something to the world:
And death's reign was already coming to an end.
The graves opened for a moment so the world would never forget what was about to happen forever.
